{"file":"/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/sol/prompt.md","result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"0a5f66","wall_time_seconds":0.000023954,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1474,"output":"Read /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/sol/package.md. It holds image section 15 (Buluşmalar) of the frozen surah commentary of surah 103: the Arabic text of the ayat concerned, the Turkish
commentary written on them, the words/roots/branch labels recorded in the frozen surah commentary, and the
whole surah in Arabic. The selected commentary defines your scope; the other inputs supply context.

Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into
one quotation. Distinguish WLC's written/ketiv stream from qere and other readings; name another witness when
you rely on it. Discovery is memory-only: the later verifier will open the actual texts and check your claims.

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

Write one TSV row per distinct connection with exactly six tab-separated fields:

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

strength: strong, medium, weak. tradition: tevrat (Hebrew Bible and Jewish literature) or incil (New Testament and
Christian literature). kind: paralel, motif, karsi_anlati, soydas, yorum_gelenegi. ref: for the Hebrew Bible and
the New Testament an edition-qualified OSIS reference, one verse per row, no ranges
(WLC:Gen.22.2, WLC:Ps.1.3, SBLGNT:Matt.6.5; consecutive verses on their own rows).
Use Hebrew WLC numbering for Hebrew Bible candidates and SBLGNT numbering for New Testament candidates;
do not silently transfer English/KJV verse numbers. For other works give the work and its place as a reader
cites it (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 22:2;
Genesis Rabbah 56:1; Berakhot 60b; Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise 5:6; Protevangelium of James 8). basis: the words,
scene or motif that carries the link, in a few words. Strongest first. Keep distinct reasons or link kinds for
one passage in separate rows; exact repeated connections are unnecessary. Do not regrade an existing row.
The handoff groups references but preserves each distinct connection for an individual verdict.

Do not write a header row, rank numbers, Markdown, sections or prose outside TSV rows. Save the rows to
/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/sol/list.tsv. End nonempty files with a newline. Zero qualifying candidates means an explicitly created
empty file. The saved file, not the chat response, is the deliverable.
"}}}

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

İmgeler birkaç sahnede üst üste biner. En geniş olanı yaşlı adamın bahçesidir {source:2:266}: hurma ve üzüm, yani sıkılacak meyve; yağmurla büyüyen ürün; ömrün geç vakti, yani asrın akşamüstü anlamı; ve sonunda aynı kökten bir kasırga. Bir ömür boyunca biriken ürünün, tam elde edileceği vakitte, sıkmanın ve yağmurun adını taşıyan kökün öteki yüzüyle yok olması, ikinci ayetin kaybını tek bir görüntüye toplar. Yusuf'un yılı ise aynı kökün iyi yüzlerini birleştirir: {ar:فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ, tr:fîhi yugâsu'n-nâsu ve fîhi ya'sirûn, gloss:o yıl insanlar yardıma kavuşur ve o yıl sıkarlar, source:12:49}; yağmur, sıkma ve kurtuluş aynı cümlededir. Yusuf'un zindanında ise sıkma ile alıkonma yan yanadır {source:12:36}, ve sabrın kendisi, acı bir sıkma özü olarak, alıkonmanın kelimesiyle aynıdır.

İkinci sahne yokuştur. Sarp yokuşa atılmak {source:90:11} bir yolculuk ve bir yük sahnesidir; yokuşun ne olduğu sorulunca {ar:فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ, tr:fekku rakabe, gloss:bir boynu çözmek, source:90:13} ve {ar:أَوْ إِطْعَٰمٌۭ فِى يَوْمٍۢ ذِى مَسْغَبَةٍۢ, tr:ev it'âmun fî yevmin zî mesgabe, gloss:ya da açlık gününde doyurmak, source:90:14} cevabı gelir; tutulan esir çözülür. Ardından karşılıklı tavsiye gelir {source:90:17}. Yük hayvanı ve yol, tutma ve salıverme, çekişmeden birlikteliğe geçiş tek bir yürüyüşte birleşir; bu, surenin üçüncü ayetindeki fiilin Kur'an'daki öteki kullanımıdır.

Üçüncü sahne vasiyet anıdır {source:5:106}: ölüm, alıkonma, yemin, vasiyet ve hak aynı ayettedir; ertesi ayette tanıklığın "daha hak" oluşu tartılır {source:5:107}. Burada tutma imgesi ile emanet imgesi buluşur, borç ayetinde de pazar ile emanet buluşur {source:2:282}. Kötü pazarlık ile ters sabır da tek ayettedir {source:2:175}: sapıklığı satın alanlar, ateşe dayanan cüretkârlardır. Tutunma ile birliktelik ise ip ayetinde birleşir {source:3:103}: hep birlikte tutunmak, düşmanların kardeş olması ve uçurumun kenarından çekilmek bir sahnedir. Örümcek evi hem sığınağın hem dokumanın karşıtıdır {source:29:41}. Soyların kesildiği an ile terazinin hafif gelmesi de art arda gelir {source:23:101}.

Bu buluşmalar surenin hareketini taşır. Birinci ayet tek kelimeyle, sıkan, saran, bağlayan ve harcanan bir zamanı anar: hem sermaye hem günün sonu, hem sıkma hem sığınak, hem yağmur hem kasırga. İkinci ayet bu zamanın içindeki insanı gösterir: ana parası eriyen, sapan, kendini tutamayan, terazide hafif gelen biri. Üçüncü ayet sahneyi tek kişiden topluluğa çevirir: iman edenler güvenliğe girer, işleri kerpiç gibi yerine oturur, birbirlerine gece ile gündüz gibi eklenirler ve el değiştiren iki şey vardır. Hak, hem borç hem sapmayan darbe hem de herkesi işiyle yüzleştiren gündür; sabır hem kendini tutmak hem kefil hem de mühürlü kapta saklanan acı ilaçtır. Sure baskı ve tükenişle açılır, birbirine iletilen ve saklanan bir özle kapanır.

*** Add File: /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/sol/list.tsv
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.40.11	Joseph's imprisoned cupbearer squeezes grapes	The commentary puts squeezing beside detention in Joseph's prison; the cupbearer presses grapes into Pharaoh's cup inside his prison dream, giving that pairing a concrete narrative scene.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.40.13	cupbearer released after three days	The commentary moves from prison's restraint to relief; Joseph tells the imprisoned cupbearer he will be restored to service, a specific release following the pressing dream.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.29	seven years of abundance	The commentary's year of provision follows Joseph's prediction; Joseph announces years of plenty before scarcity, making productive time something to preserve.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.30	seven years of famine	The commentary pairs the fruitful year with threatened loss; Joseph says famine will consume the prior abundance, turning accumulated yield into a question of survival.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.36	food stored against famine	The commentary's rain, pressing and rescue culminate in usable provision; Joseph proposes keeping grain so the land will not perish in famine.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	death on the night stored goods seem secure	The commentary's old gardener loses a lifetime's yield when it should become useful; the rich fool is called to die just after planning to store his crop, and the question asks who receives it.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.58.6	loose bonds and free oppressed people	The commentary explains the hard ascent by undoing a captive's neck; Isaiah defines the chosen fast by undoing unjust bonds and sending the oppressed free.

+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.12	threefold cord withstands rupture	The commentary's rope joins grasping, company and rescue from an edge; Ecclesiastes' cord of three strands makes solidarity itself resistant to breaking.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.8.14	trust like a spider's web	The commentary sets the spider house against real refuge; Bildad describes the godless person's confidence as a spider's web, making apparently woven support precarious.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.27	rain, floods and wind bring down a house	The commentary's shelter image fails under destructive weather; Jesus' house built on sand collapses when rain, floods and wind strike it.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.47.29	dying Jacob binds Joseph by oath	The commentary's testament scene unites death, custody and sworn duty; dying Jacob requires Joseph's pledged hand and loyal burial promise.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.19.15	two witnesses establish a matter	The commentary's deathbed testament weighs witnesses and the truer claim; Deuteronomy requires two or three witnesses for a matter to stand.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.21.13	false sworn witnesses cause Naboth's death	The commentary's testament scene makes truth in testimony decisive; two men testify falsely against Naboth and he is killed, showing the stakes of a corrupt witness.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.9.16	death required in a testament argument	The commentary combines death and entrusted last instructions; Hebrews treats a testament as requiring the death of its maker in its covenant argument.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.9.17	testament operative after death	The commentary's bequest becomes urgent at death; Hebrews says a testament takes effect upon death, sharpening the relation between dying and transfer.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.10	creditor must not enter debtor's house for pledge	The commentary joins marketplace debt with custody of an entrusted thing; Deuteronomy restrains the lender's power over a pledged object.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.13	return pledged cloak before sunset	The commentary's debt meets the passing day and the duty to return what was held; the lender must give back the poor debtor's cloak by sunset so he can sleep in it.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.22.27	debtor's bed taken for lack of payment	The commentary imagines capital eroding and security forfeited in a bad transaction; Proverbs asks why a guarantor would risk having even his bed seized.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.18.27	master releases debtor and cancels loan	The commentary puts restraint, debt and release in one scene; the master lets a servant go and forgives an unpayable debt.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.18.28	forgiven debtor seizes his debtor by the throat	The commentary's holding image collides with a debt transaction; a newly forgiven servant physically grips another servant and demands repayment.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.18.30	unmerciful creditor jails debtor	The commentary joins debt, confinement and the choice to release; the servant instead casts his fellow servant into prison until payment.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.25.33	Esau sells his birthright	The commentary's bad purchase exchanges lasting value for ruinous immediate gain; Esau swears away his birthright for the meal offered by Jacob.

+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Josh.2.18	scarlet cord marks a house for rescue	The commentary's rope combines attachment with group safety at a deadly edge; Rahab is told to bind a scarlet cord in the window and gather her family in the house.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Josh.2.19	family must remain inside the cord-marked house	The commentary moves from individual grasp to shared safety; Rahab's household is safe within the marked house but not if members go outside.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.2	bear one another's burdens	The commentary's steep path becomes a shared journey with a load; Paul commands the community to carry one another's burdens.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.3.13	exhort one another every day	The commentary reads the last verse as reciprocal transfer across passing time; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation so no one hardens through sin.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	consider how to stir love and good works	The commentary passes counsel into fitting deeds within a group; Hebrews asks people to consider one another so love and good works result.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.25	assemble and encourage as the day approaches	The commentary's people preserve each other through diminishing time toward a decisive day; Hebrews connects gathering, mutual encouragement and the approaching day.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.11	encourage and build each other up	The commentary says people fit together like building material and pass counsel between them; Paul tells them to encourage one another and build each other up.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.14	admonish, help weak and be patient with all	The commentary pairs reciprocal advice with patience and care for vulnerable people; Paul joins these commands in one instruction to the community.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.2	entrust teaching to people who will teach others	The commentary's truth and patience are handed onward and kept; Timothy must entrust received teaching to reliable people able to teach still others.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.1.14	guard the entrusted good deposit	The commentary ends with an essence kept and passed rather than spent; Timothy is ordered to guard a received deposit through the Holy Spirit.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.7	patient farmer waits for precious crop and rains	The commentary ties patience to rain, fruit, useful yield and passing time; James makes a farmer waiting for rains and harvest the model for patient endurance.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.8.15	hold word and bear fruit with endurance	The commentary joins holding, fruitful work and sabr as kept substance; Jesus' good soil consists of hearers who hold the word and bear fruit through endurance.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.12	endurance, commandments and faith together	The commentary closes with faith, right deeds and patience held by a people; Revelation calls for the endurance of saints who keep God's commands and faith in Jesus.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.13.10	captivity and endurance of the saints	The commentary makes holding and captivity meet patience; Revelation speaks of captivity and immediately names the endurance and faith of the saints.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.5.27	weighed in scales and found wanting	The commentary pairs severed supports with light weight in the final balance; Daniel's verdict on Belshazzar finds him deficient when weighed.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	dead judged by written record of works	The commentary moves from broken lineage and light scales to a day confronting each person with deeds; the dead stand for judgment according to what is recorded of their works.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.12.11	painful discipline later yields righteous fruit	The commentary treats patience as a bitter essence preserved for benefit; Hebrews says discipline hurts now yet later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.6	faithful friend's wounds	The commentary imagines true counsel as an unpleasant medicine retained for good; Proverbs values the wounds of a faithful friend over an enemy's plentiful kisses.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.5	living stones built into one house	The commentary likens fitting good works and joined believers to building blocks; Peter describes believers as living stones being built into a spiritual house.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.2.22	people built together into a dwelling	The commentary says individuals fit into one community like placed bricks; Paul says his addressees are built together into a dwelling for God.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.11.14	rain supports grain, wine and oil	The commentary's garden links rain to produce that can be pressed; Deuteronomy promises seasonal rain so grain, wine and oil can be gathered, without Joseph's explicit rescue scene.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Joel.2.24	threshing floors full and vats overflow	The commentary's good side of the year is stored produce and pressing; Joel imagines restored abundance filling floors with grain and vats with wine and oil.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Joel.2.25	years consumed by locusts restored	The commentary pictures a lifetime's accumulated crop erased; Joel answers lost productive years with a promise to restore what successive locust swarms consumed.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.5.6	vineyard deprived of rain after judgment	The commentary's rain-grown garden can be lost in a single turn; Isaiah's judged vineyard is denied rain after its owner abandons its care, a reversed weather detail.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.18	barns enlarged to store harvest	The commentary treats late accumulated fruit as vulnerable capital; the rich fool builds larger barns for all his grain and goods just before the death sentence in Luke 12:20.

+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.15.14	provision from flock, threshing floor and winepress	The commentary links freeing a captive with feeding and pressed yield; Deuteronomy orders gifts from animals, grain and winepress to the departing servant.
